title: Red and green will-o’-the-wisps and danger signals.
html_source:
A will-o'-the-wisp painted by Arnold Böcklin (1882), via Wikimedia Commons.

Will-o'-the-wisps are still-unexplained transient lights reported by old travelers—they form a big part of European folklore. They’re generally seen to be bad omens; some strains of myth depict them as souls rejected from Hell.

Don Gifford in Ulysses Annotated draws a connection with the will-o'-the-wisp in Goethe’s Faust:

In Goethe’s Faust (I.xxi), a will-o'-the-wisp lights the way up the “magic-mad” mountain as Faust and Mephistopheles make their way toward the Walpurgisnacht (Witches' Sabbath) assembly. (p.452)

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: It might be helpful to point out how appropriate it is to begin the episode with reference to the “danger signals” the will-o-the-wisps provide inasmuch as they light the way up the hill Ignis Fatuus in Faust describes as “magic-mad tonight.” “Magic-mad” fairly describes the phantasmagoric journey on which Joyce takes the reader in these pages.
